title_en: Li et al. v. Shao et al. — dispute over confirmation of contract invalidity
ruling_gist_en: Where a trust trustee transfers its position as trustee under the trust relationship without the consent of the settlor, this seriously undermines the trust foundation. In the absence of the settlor's consent or ratification, from the perspective of strengthening the trustee's fiduciary duty and protecting the settlor's interests from infringement, the settlor in the trust relationship should be granted a right of choice. If the settlor does not consent to the transfer or refuses to ratify it, the transfer is void.
keywords_en: Civil; Dispute over confirmation of invalidity of contract; First instance; Supreme People's Court; Beijing City; Natural person; Legal person; Contract Law; Validity of trustee's unauthorized transfer of status; Impact of settlor's consent or ratification on transfer; Determination of malicious collusion; Trust relationship; Transfer of trustee status; Employee incentive trust; Good faith; Dispute with Shao et al. over confirmation of invalidity of contract
full_text_en:
Li, et al. v. Shao, et al. — dispute over confirmation of invalidity of contract

Ruling Gist

Where a trustee of a trust, without the consent of the trust settlor, unilaterally transfers its position as trustee under the trust relationship, thereby seriously undermining the basis of trust in the trust, and in the absence of the settlor's consent or ratification, from the perspective of reinforcing the fiduciary duty of the trustee and protecting the settlor's interests from infringement, the settlor under the trust relationship should be granted a right of election. Where the settlor does not consent to the transfer or refuses to ratify it, the transfer act is invalid.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2022) Zui Gao Fa Shang Chu No. 7

Plaintiff: Li, residing at Haidian District, Beijing, the People's Republic of China.

Agent ad litem: Huang Zifeng, lawyer at Beijing Horizon Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Chen Xiao, lawyer at Beijing Horizon Law Firm.

Plaintiff: Mou Technology Group Co., Ltd. Domicile: Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area, the People's Republic of China.

Legal representative: Xu, Co-President of the company.

Agent ad litem: Huang Zifeng, lawyer at Beijing Horizon Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Chen Xiao, lawyer at Beijing Horizon Law Firm.

Defendant: Shao, residing at Haidian District, Beijing, the People's Republic of China.

Agent ad litem: He Haifeng, lawyer at Beijing Tian Tong Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Chen Haoxin, lawyer at Beijing Tian Tong Law Firm.

Defendant: Mou Investment Co., Ltd. (P*Ltd.). Domicile: Road Town, Tortola, VG1110, British Virgin Islands.

Representative: Luo, Director of the company.

Agent ad litem: Yin Chao, lawyer at Beijing Zhongdun Law Firm.

In the case concerning the dispute over confirmation of invalidity of contract between plaintiffs Li and Mou Technology Group Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Mou Technology Company) and defendants Shao and Mou Investment Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Mou Investment Company), the Beijing No. 4 Intermediate People's Court (hereinafter referred to as Beijing No. 4 Intermediate Court) accepted the case on November 10, 2021. Pursuant to Article 39, paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (2021 Amendment) and Article 2, item 5 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Establishment of International Commercial Courts, this Court rendered the civil ruling (2022) Zui Gao Fa Min Xia No. 50 on March 21, 2022, deciding that this case shall be tried by the Second International Commercial Court of this Court. After the case was docketed on June 24, 2022, this Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law and held a public hearing on April 27, 2023. Plaintiffs Li and Mou Technology Company's agents ad litem Huang Zifeng and Chen Xiao, defendant Shao and his agent ad litem Wu Taojun (changed to Chen Haoxin after the hearing), and Mou Investment Company's agent ad litem Yin Chao appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. This case has now been concluded.

Li and Mou Technology Company filed the lawsuit, requesting: 1. A judgment declaring that the "Agreement on the Assignment of the Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement" (with a financial management amount of USD 50 million, hereinafter referred to as the "Assignment Agreement (USD 50 Million)") signed by Shao and Mou Investment Company is invalid; 2. All litigation costs, including the case acceptance fee and preservation fee, to be borne by Shao and Mou Investment Company. Main facts and reasons: Mou Investment Company is the entity holding and operating employee incentive assets of Mou Technology Company, with a paid-in registered capital of USD 1. The sole shareholder and legal representative is Luo. In August 2009, Mou Technology Company, along with representatives of incentivized employees, Mou Investment Company, and a third party Ace*Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Company A), jointly negotiated and signed the "Charter of the Trust Rights Committee" (hereinafter referred to as the "Trust Charter"), and accordingly established the Trust Rights Committee (hereinafter referred to as the Committee). According to the Trust Charter, Mou Investment Company and Company A were required to establish trust relationships with incentivized employees selected by Mou Technology Company, sign the "Trust Contract," hold and operate employee incentive assets as trustees, and distribute trust rights to the incentivized employees (i.e., the trust settlors) in accordance with the Trust Contract. The assets held and managed by Mou Investment Company consisted of three parts: first, the registered capital of USD 1 contributed by the sole shareholder Luo; second, the employee incentive assets granted by Mou Technology Company for its operation and management; and third, the stock rights formed from the original employee shares of the incentivized employees (i.e., trust settlors) and the subscription payments for trust assets made by them. As one of Mou Technology Company's incentivized employees, Li signed the Trust Contract with Mou Investment Company and Company A in July 2013, becoming a trust settlor and beneficiary under Mou Investment Company, and paid RMB 200,000 as subscription payment for trust assets in accordance with the Trust Contract, thereby obtaining the corresponding trust rights as stipulated in the Trust Contract and the Trust Charter. Shao previously served as Chairman of the Board of Mou Technology Company, Committee member and Chairperson, among other positions, and was responsible for the long-term implementation of the employee incentive plan, holding key items such as Mou Investment Company's certificates, seals, and chops. After Shao was removed from the Chairman position due to poor performance, he demanded that Luo transfer all rights and obligations of Mou Investment Company to him, on the pretext of facilitating the implementation of the employee incentive plan. On November 13, 2020, Luo, on behalf of Mou Investment Company, signed the "Agreement on the Assignment of Rights and Obligations of Mou Investment Co., Ltd." (hereinafter referred to as the "Agreement on Assigning Company Rights and Obligations"), the "Agreement on the Assignment of the Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement" (with a financial management amount of USD 18 million, hereinafter referred to as the "Assignment Agreement (USD 18 Million)"), and the Assignment Agreement (USD 50 Million) involved in this case, transferring all rights and obligations related to the USD 50 million entrusted investment and financial management under the "Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement" signed between Mou Investment Company and a third party, Jin (Chim*, a Singapore citizen), to Shao for free. The said funds and their investment returns and other property rights belong to employee incentive assets. Without the consent of Li and Mou Technology Company, Mou Investment Company and Shao, by taking advantage of their positions, signed the above agreements, constituting malicious unauthorized disposal, seriously violating the provisions of the Trust Contract and the Trust Charter, weakening the ability of the trustee Mou Investment Company to perform trust rights distribution, causing Mou Technology Company's goal of retaining talent through trust incentives to fail, and objectively and seriously infringing upon the lawful rights and interests of Li and Mou Technology Company. Pursuant to Article 52, item 2 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the "Contract Law"), the said assignment agreement shall be deemed invalid.

Shao argued: This case should be suspended or the plaintiffs' lawsuit should be dismissed. (1) Regarding the three agreements signed by Mou Investment Company and Shao — the Agreement on Assigning Company Rights and Obligations, the Assignment Agreement (USD 18 Million), and the Assignment Agreement (USD 50 Million) — the plaintiffs filed three separate lawsuits. Among them, the lawsuit filed with the Beijing No. 4 Intermediate Court concerning the Agreement on Assigning Company Rights and Obligations includes the subject matter to be tried in both case No. (2022) Zui Gao Fa Shang Chu No. 7 and case No. (2022) Zui Gao Fa Shang Chu No. 8, thus constituting duplicate litigation. Moreover, Mou Technology Company did not sign the Trust Contract, does not hold trust rights against Mou Investment Company, and has never contributed any assets; therefore, it has no interest in this case. Accordingly, the plaintiffs' lawsuit should be dismissed. (2) The trust involved in this case has a dual trust structure. All stocks under Mou Investment Company's name have been sold, and the relevant funds have been fully used to distribute to employees who have withdrawn from the trust. Mou Investment Company's obligations have been fully performed. The stocks under the name of the other trustee, Company A, have never been sold. Therefore, the remaining trust settlors' trust rights can only be asserted against Company A, and Li no longer holds any rights against Mou Investment Company. The agreements in question do not harm Li's rights and interests. Furthermore, the issue of whether Li holds rights against Mou Investment Company should be arbitrated by a Hong Kong arbitral institution in accordance with the Trust Contract, and the court has no jurisdiction to review it. (3) Although the trustee under the Trust Contract signed by Li was Mou Investment Company and Company A, the parties had reached an agreement at the time of signing that Mou Investment Company would be the nominal trustee and Shao the actual trustee. The Agreement on Assigning Company Rights and Obligations merely confirmed the true legal relationship among the parties. Before and after the signing of the agreements in question, Shao actively performed his obligations and never harmed Li's interests. If Li wishes to withdraw from the trust and receive distribution, Shao will also perform the contractual obligations in accordance with the agreement. (4) Li argued that the agreements in question are invalid on the grounds of malicious collusion, but failed to provide evidence that Mou Investment Company and Shao had the intent to maliciously collude to harm Li's rights and interests. In the evidence submitted by the plaintiffs to the Beijing No. 4 Intermediate Court, i.e., Exhibit 9 "Explanation of Circumstances," it was already clarified that Mou Investment Company only became aware of the potential harm to Li's rights and interests after signing the agreements in question. The plaintiffs have already admitted that Mou Investment Company and Shao did not have the intent to maliciously collude to harm the interests of a third party at the time of signing the agreements.

Mou Investment Company argued: Mou Investment Company is a trust platform established by Mou Technology Company for employee incentives, with the nominal shareholder being one of Mou Technology Company's founders. After the trust establishment meeting in 2009, although two trust platforms were contracted, distributions and payments were all made using assets under Mou Investment Company's name. Mou Investment Company originally held stocks of Mou Technology Company's U.S. listed entity, but later sold all of them to entrust for investment and financial management. Before signing the assignment agreements in question, apart from the trust subscription funds, the main trust assets under Mou Investment Company's name were the two investment and financial management funds of USD 50 million and USD 18 million. In early November 2020, Shao, then Committee Chairperson, approached Luo, the sole shareholder and director of Mou Investment Company, mentioning that he had been removed from the Chairman position. A week later, Shao approached Luo again, stating that Luo needed to sign several agreements on behalf of Mou Investment Company so that Shao could handle subsequent matters with full authority. Although Luo felt it was somewhat inappropriate, he did not give it much thought and signed the agreements accordingly. Mou Investment Company is not the actual right holder of the assets transferred under the agreements in question; it is only authorized to manage the trust assets for distribution and payment to its employees. The assignment agreements in question harmed the plaintiffs' interests. Mou Investment Company acknowledges that it should not have transferred the trust asset rights and interests to Shao for free and then signed the agreements; it was at fault. However, Shao was the one who benefited and should bear primary responsibility. Mou Investment Company is unwilling to bear the litigation costs. As to the validity of the assignment agreements in question, it requests the court to determine in accordance with the law.

Based on the evidence submitted by the parties and examined through cross-examination — including the Trust Charter, the Trust Contract and its attached Trust Rights Record Form and Receipt, the Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreements (two copies), the Agreement on Assigning Company Rights and Obligations, the Assignment Agreement (USD 18 Million), the Assignment Agreement (USD 50 Million), the Shareholder Resolution of Mou Technology Company and the Board Resolution of Mou Technology Company, relevant bank statements, emails, WeChat chat records, bank transfer vouchers, and trust rights payment confirmation letters — this Court finds the following facts:

Mou Investment Company is the entity holding and operating employee incentive assets of Mou Technology Company. It was incorporated on August 19, 2005, in the British Virgin Islands, with a paid-in registered capital of USD 1, and Luo was its sole shareholder and legal representative.

In August 2009, representatives of Mou Technology Company's employees, acting as trust settlors, together with Mou Technology Company, Mou Investment Company, and Company A, negotiated and signed the Trust Charter, and accordingly established the Committee. The Trust Charter was formulated on August 27, 2009, and amended on October 11, 2012. Article 3.1 of the Trust Charter provides: The trust assets are the stock rights arising from the HOLI stocks of Mou Technology Company's Nasdaq-listed entity contributed by the trustee, forming the trust assets, i.e., trust rights. Article 4.1 provides: The Committee is the authorized management body for the trust rights, and its authority derives from the authorization of the trust settlors, the trustee, and a third party. The Committee consists of nine members: seven representatives of the trust settlors, one representative of the company, and one representative of the trustee, with a chairperson elected through consultation among the members. Pursuant to Article 4.3, the Committee has the power to approve and execute plans for subscription, exchange, allotment, distribution, payment, and withdrawal of trust stock rights; to accept, review, and assist in executing trust settlors' applications for realizing trust rights; and to accept and resolve disputes and disagreements arising from trust rights. Article 5.1 provides: The Committee shall determine the total amount for subscription or exchange, subscription price, start date, conversion ratio, etc., based on current needs and the situation of the listed company's stocks. Article 5.2 provides: The Committee determines the maximum amount each employee may subscribe; employees subscribe voluntarily, without coercion or apportionment. Article 5.4 provides: Subscribers shall pay subscription funds to the person and company designated by the trustee within the time limit specified by the Committee based on the authorized subscription amount determined by Mou Technology Company (third party). Failure to pay the full subscription funds within the time limit shall be deemed automatic waiver, and the subscription quota will not be retained, but does not affect future subscriptions for increases or allotments. Article 6.1 provides: Trust assets are strictly prohibited from private transactions or transfers. The Committee deems any private transaction or transfer improper and invalid, and will not recognize or settle any private transaction. The Committee has the power to make and execute decisions based on the actual circumstances.

On July 15, 2013, Li, as the trust settlor, Mou Investment Company and Company A as the trustees, and Mou Technology Company as the third party, entered into a Trust Contract. Pursuant to Articles 1.2 and 1.6 of the contract, trust assets refer to the assets delivered by the trust settlor to the trustee for management based on trust. In this contract, it refers to the stock rights of Mou Technology Company's Nasdaq ticker symbol HOLI obtained by Li during his employment at Mou Technology Company in accordance with certain rules. Stock rights are the trust settlor's trust assets, not stocks, but the benefits arising from HOLI stocks, i.e., the value of the benefits. Article 1.12 provides that the Committee is an institution jointly authorized by the trust settlors, the trustee, and the third party to coordinate the rights and obligations among the three parties. Within the scope of authorization, it has the power to formulate documents for generating trust rights, operating rules, withdrawal mechanisms, and other powers determined in accordance with the charter. Article 1.5 provides that the "third party" is the person who limits the trust settlor's stock rights. The trust settlor is subject to such restrictions on a completely voluntary basis, and such restrictions constitute the basis for generating trust assets, which originate from the third party. Article 1.7 provides that the trustee means the person who manages the trust settlor's stock rights in its own name based on the trust settlor's trust. In this contract, the specific subjects are Mou Investment Company and Company A. Article 3.2.1 provides: "The trust assets under this contract are the stock rights of 10,000 full shares of HOLI. The start date of the trust rights is August 1, 2013." Article 3.4.4 provides: "When a non-trust settlor and beneficiary claims the trust assets, and the trustee does not receive an effective response from the trust settlor within a reasonable time, the trustee has the right to handle the stock rights in accordance with established rules and deposit the value of the handled rights into a custodial or notarial institution, with the costs incurred to be paid from the stock rights." Articles 5.2 to 5.3 provide that in the event of the trustee's death or inability to normally perform trust business, the trustee shall designate a lawyer or other custodial institution to perform on its behalf. The above matters must be confirmed by the Committee established by the three parties under the contract. Regarding the status and related rights and obligations of the third party and Mou Technology Company, Articles 6.1 to 6.4 further provide that the third party is not a party to the trust relationship but merely the setter of the conditions for generating the trust. The third party restricts the trust settlor in accordance with the following standards and conditions: the trust settlor's working hours, position, performance, and conduct; the third party's rules and regulations; and the established rules formulated with the participation of the third party. The third party has no right to restrict the trust settlor's rights beyond the standards and conditions. The third party shall immediately give relevant comments upon receiving relevant applications. On the same day, Li paid RMB 200,000 to the trustee as trust rights payment.

On February 22, 2016, Mou Investment Company, as the entrusting party, and Jin, as the entrusted party, signed an Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement in Singapore, stipulating: Whereas the entrusting party has its own funds and seeks project investment and financial management appreciation, and the entrusted party has investment and financial management channels, the entrusting party will invest USD 50 million in the entrusted party for project investment and financial management, with an investment term of five years. The entrusting party has the right to review investment projects and financial management conditions and to obtain all investment and financial management returns. The entrusted party shall ensure the safety of the investment and regularly report the investment and return status to the entrusting party. The entrusted party is entitled to corresponding compensation based on the returns. The agreement also stipulated circumstances under which the entrusting party has the right to withdraw funds. The agreement also provided that Shao is the fully authorized agent of the entrusting party. The agreement is governed by Singapore law, and disputes are to be submitted to the Singapore International Arbitration Centre for resolution. Luo, representing Mou Investment Company, and Jin signed the agreement, and Shao signed as the agent of the entrusting party.

On March 4, 2016, Mou Investment Company, as the entrusting party, and Shao, as the entrusted party, signed an Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement in Singapore, with an investment amount of USD 18 million. Apart from that, the remainder of the agreement was identical to the agreement dated February 22, 2016. Luo, representing Mou Investment Company, and Shao signed the agreement.

On November 13, 2020, Mou Investment Company, as the assignor, and Shao, as the assignee, signed an Agreement on Assigning Company Rights and Obligations in Beijing. Article 2.1 stipulates: "The assignor agrees that all rights and obligations of P*Ltd. shall be transferred in their entirety to the assignee as of the date of signing this agreement, and no other person's claim to such rights shall be accepted." Article 2.2 stipulates: "The assignee agrees to assume all rights and obligations of P*Ltd., and the assignor shall no longer bear related obligations."

On the same day, Mou Investment Company, as the assignor, and Shao, as the assignee, signed the Assignment Agreement (USD 18 Million). Article 1 stipulates: "On February 22, 2016, the assignor and the assignee signed the Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement, and the assignor remitted USD 18 million to the assignee for investment and financial management." Article 2.1 stipulates: "The assignor agrees that all rights and obligations of Party A (i.e., Mou Investment Company, hereinafter the same) under the Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement shall be transferred in their entirety to the assignee as of the date of signing this agreement, and no other person's claim to such rights shall be accepted." Article 2.2 stipulates: "The assignee agrees to assume all rights and obligations of Party A under the Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement, and the assignor shall no longer bear related obligations."

Same day, a certain investment company, as the transferor, also entered into the "Transfer Agreement (USD 50 Million)" with the transferee Shao and the third party Jin. Article 1 stipulated: "On March 4, 2016, the transferor and the third party entered into the 'Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement,' and the transferor remitted USD 50 million to the third party for investment and financial management, and entrusted the transferee as the full agent." Article 2.1 stipulated: "The transferor agrees that all rights and obligations of Party A under the 'Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement' shall be transferred in full to the transferee from the date of signing this agreement, and shall not accept any claims of rights from any other person (including the third party)." Article 2.2 stipulated: "The transferee agrees to accept all rights and obligations of Party A under the 'Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement,' and the transferor shall no longer bear relevant obligations."

Shao and Luo signed the above three transfer agreements on behalf of the investment company.

On July 8, 2020, the sole shareholder of a certain technology company, Beijing XX Co., Ltd., made the fifth shareholder decision of 2020 for such technology company, removing Shao from his positions as chairman, legal representative, and director of the company and the technology company, and appointing Ma as chairman and legal representative of the company and the technology company. On the same day, the first meeting of the board of directors of 2020 of the technology company made a decision to remove Shao from his position as general manager of the company and to appoint Xu as the company's general manager.

Luo, the sole shareholder and director of the investment company, submitted a "Statement of Facts" to the court on April 23, 2021, which stated: The sole purpose of the investment company's operation and existence was to provide incentives for key employees of the technology company and its affiliated enterprises using all its assets as a vehicle; some key employees had already received incentives and entered into "Trust Contracts" with the investment company, and the incentive assets were still managed by the investment company. For many years, this work was handled by Shao, who was then the chairman of the technology company. Luo had great trust in Shao, and the daily management of the trust matters handled by the investment company was the responsibility of Shao, who also held the seals, licenses, and other documents. On November 13, 2020, Shao found Luo and stated that the employee incentive matters had always been handled by him, and the assets of the investment company had been fully disposed of, so it was necessary to close the investment company. To facilitate the process, it was necessary to transfer all rights and obligations of the investment company to him free of charge, requesting Luo to sign the three agreements involved in the case prepared in advance. Since the investment company's trust property had been managed and operated by Shao since 2009, and Luo had been retired from the technology company for many years, Luo cooperated and signed the three agreements involved without much thought. After some time, a company employee contacted Luo, stating that Shao had been removed from his position as chairman in July 2020 and had since been plotting to take the employee trust property for himself, and that the purpose of his signing the agreements with the investment company was to implement this plot. Luo then realized that the three agreements he had signed actually infringed upon the interests of the numerous trustees working for the technology company and its affiliated enterprises, as well as the interests of employees eligible to receive such trust property incentives in the future, and should be null and void.

It was also found that Li and the technology company did not apply for property preservation, and there were no expenses for preservation.

The court holds: The investment company was established in the British Virgin Islands. Pursuant to Article 1, Item 1 of the "Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Choice of Law for Foreign-Related Civil Relations (I)" and Article 3 of the "Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Establishment of International Commercial Courts," this case is a commercial case involving foreign elements. Article 8 of the "Law of the People's Republic of China on Choice of Law for Foreign-Related Civil Relations" stipulates: "The characterization of a foreign-related civil relationship shall be governed by the law of the forum." Li and the technology company alleged that the investment company and Shao, without their consent, took advantage of their positions to sign the "Agreement on the Transfer of the Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement," constituting malicious unauthorized disposition, which seriously harmed the legitimate rights and interests of Li and the technology company. According to Article 52, Item 2 of the "Contract Law," such transfer agreement should be deemed invalid. Shao argued that there was no malicious collusion between him and the investment company. Based on the parties' allegations and defenses, and considering Article 52, Item 2 of the "Contract Law" (effective at the time of the parties' actions), this case is a dispute over confirmation of contract invalidity. Regarding the applicable law in this case, Plaintiff Li invoked the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China as the legal basis for his lawsuit. During the court hearing, all parties indicated that the laws of the People's Republic of China should apply to this case. According to Article 3 of the "Law on Choice of Law for Foreign-Related Civil Relations," which states that "the parties may, in accordance with the law, expressly choose the law applicable to a foreign-related civil relationship," the laws of the People's Republic of China shall apply to this case.

Based on the claims of Li and the technology company, and in light of the defenses of Shao and the investment company, the main issues in dispute in this case are: 1. Whether the technology company is a proper plaintiff in this case; 2. Whether this case constitutes a duplicate lawsuit with the other case being heard by the Beijing No. 4 Intermediate People's Court; 3. Whether this case should be premised on Li enjoying trust rights; 4. Whether the defendant maliciously colluded to harm the plaintiff's interests; 5. The determination of the validity of the "Transfer Agreement (USD 50 Million)."

I. Standing of the Technology Company

Shao argued that the technology company did not sign the "Trust Contract," never contributed any property, had no trust rights over the investment company, and had no stake in this case, so the lawsuit by the technology company should be dismissed. The technology company argued that the trust involved established a long-term continuous incentive mechanism for outstanding employees, and the transfer agreement harmed the interests of existing and future incentivized employees, thereby harming the technology company's interests. It had the right to file this lawsuit. The court holds: According to Article 122, Item 1 of the "Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China" (2023 Amendment), the plaintiff must have a direct stake in the case as one of the conditions for filing a lawsuit. In this case, although Article 6.1 of the "Trust Contract" states that the technology company is not a party to the trust relationship, the technology company appears as a third party in the "Trust Contract" and is a signatory to the agreement. Moreover, Article 1.5 of the contract stipulates that the technology company is the party that restricts the stock rights of the trustees, and the trustees are subject to such restrictions on a purely voluntary basis. These restrictions are the basis for the generation of the trust property, which originates from the technology company. Articles 6.2 to 6.4 of the "Trust Contract" further stipulate the relevant rights and obligations of the technology company. Since the purpose of establishing the investment company was to incentivize employees of the technology company and its affiliated companies, and its operations since establishment have only involved the subscription of trust property and the cashing out of trust interests according to the "Trust Charter" and "Trust Contract," the operational status of the investment company may affect the incentivization of employees of the technology company and, accordingly, have a certain impact on the actual interests of the technology company. The technology company believes that the transfer agreement signed by the investment company and Shao affects the operation of the trust mechanism, impacts the incentives for employees of the technology company and its affiliated companies, and thus harms its own interests. It therefore filed this lawsuit as the plaintiff. The court holds that the technology company is a proper plaintiff in this case.

II. Whether This Case Constitutes a Duplicate Lawsuit with the Case Heard by the Beijing No. 4 Intermediate People's Court

On November 13, 2020, the investment company and Shao entered into three agreements: the "Agreement on the Transfer of Company Rights and Obligations," the "Transfer Agreement (USD 18 Million)," and the "Transfer Agreement (USD 50 Million)." Li and the technology company filed three separate lawsuits regarding these three agreements. The case before this court concerns disputes over the validity of the "Transfer Agreement (USD 18 Million)" and the "Transfer Agreement (USD 50 Million)," while the other case before the Beijing No. 4 Intermediate People's Court concerns the "Agreement on the Transfer of Company Rights and Obligations." Shao argued that the case before the Beijing No. 4 Intermediate People's Court constitutes a duplicate lawsuit with this case. The court holds: The "Agreement on the Transfer of Company Rights and Obligations" involves the transfer of all rights and obligations of the investment company. Generally, once a company is established and operations commence, profits or losses continuously occur, and the value or scope of its managed property continuously changes. The investment company is still in existence, and the value or scope of its property is also continuously changing. The rights and obligations under the "Agreement on the Transfer of Company Rights and Obligations" are not necessarily identical to those under the transfer agreements involved in this case. Shao did not provide evidence to show whether the overall transfer of rights and obligations of the investment company is exactly equivalent to the transfer of rights and obligations related to the entrusted management matters of the investment company. With regard to the wording of the relevant transfer agreement, the "Agreement on the Transfer of Company Rights and Obligations" only mentions that "the property of the investment company has been properly disposed of according to the settlor's requirements." Shao also did not provide evidence to show whether such "property" is exactly equivalent to the USD 18 million and USD 50 million entrusted for financial management. Based on the existing evidence in this case, the case pending before the Beijing No. 4 Intermediate People's Court does not constitute a duplicate lawsuit with this case, but it may be related to the outcome of this case. The Beijing No. 4 Intermediate People's Court may await the outcome of this case.

III. Whether This Case Should Be Premised on Li Enjoying Trust Rights

The "Trust Contract" signed by Li and the investment company contains an arbitration clause in Hong Kong. Based on this, Shao argued that the issue of whether Li enjoys trust rights should first be arbitrated in Hong Kong. The court holds: Li alleges that the signing of the "Transfer Agreement (USD 50 Million)" by the investment company and Shao harmed his interests. Although whether Li enjoys trust rights under the contract is one of the prerequisites for determining whether his trust rights have been harmed and whether he is a proper plaintiff, the "Trust Contract" clearly identifies Li as a trustee. The technology company and the investment company, the other two parties to the "Trust Contract," have no objection to Li enjoying trust rights under the agreement, and at trial, they both stated that there was no dispute regarding Li's trust rights under the agreement. Shao, as a non-contracting party outside the "Trust Contract," argues that a party to the contract does not enjoy rights under the agreement, and that the parties must resolve this issue, which is undisputed among them, through arbitration proceedings. This argument is completely without legal basis. In fact, in his post-trial submissions, Shao also conceded that "all other trustees (including Li) paid subscription funds to Shao, and Shao paid dividends and cash-outs to them," indicating that he also effectively recognized that Li enjoys trust rights. In summary, the court does not support Shao's defense on this point.

IV. Whether the Defendant Maliciously Colluded to Harm the Plaintiff's Interests

Li and the technology company alleged that the investment company and Shao engaged in malicious collusion harming their interests, as provided under Article 52, Item 2 of the "Contract Law." The court holds: The malicious collusion referred to in Article 52, Item 2 of the "Contract Law" means that the parties to a contract, through express or implied communication of intent, collude with each other to commit acts that harm the lawful interests of others. Subjectively, malicious collusion requires a clear communication of intent between the parties to harm the lawful interests of others. It can manifest as mutual cooperation, i.e., the parties reaching an agreement in advance, or as one party making a manifestation of intent and the other party, knowing its unlawful purpose, accepting it impliedly. Objectively, it requires the actual commission of acts that harm or are sufficient to harm the lawful interests of others. Additionally, the colluding parties often seek to obtain benefits.

Article 52, Item 2 of the "Contract Law" establishes the general principle that contracts harming the interests of others through malicious collusion are void. This case involves a trust transaction background, and judgment can be made with reference to relevant provisions of the "Trust Law of the People's Republic of China" (hereinafter "Trust Law") and the provisions of the "Contract Law" governing mandate contracts, combined with the nature, content, and performance of the contracts.

(A) The Substance of the Transfer of the "Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement" Signed by the Investment Company and Shao

In 2016, the investment company entered into the "Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement" with Jin, entrusting USD 50 million in trust property to Jin for financial management. Shao, as the full agent of the investment company, also signed the agreement. The court holds: The investment company's signing of the "Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement" with Jin was an act of managing the trust property for the benefit of Li by entrusting the trust property to Jin for financial management. This entrusted financial management act was a performance of its fiduciary obligations under the "Trust Contract." This method of managing trust property does not violate Article 30, Paragraph 1 of the "Trust Law," which requires the trustee to handle trust affairs personally. When the investment company signed the agreement with Shao in November 2020, transferring the "Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement" to Shao, it meant that the principal under the original agreement was no longer the investment company but Shao. Consequently, the right to review investment projects and financial management conditions, receive all investment and financial management income, and make withdrawal decisions under specified circumstances was no longer held by the investment company but by Shao. If Jin also recognized this transfer, the obligations that Jin originally owed to the investment company to ensure investment safety and regularly report investment and income conditions would shift to Shao. Therefore, the substance of the transfer involved was that the investment company transferred its principal status under the "Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement" to Shao. Since all parties recognized that the property under the "Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement" was the trust property, the signing of the transfer agreement meant for the trustee Li that the trust matters he had entrusted to the investment company were effectively sub-entrusted by the investment company to Shao, constituting a transfer of the trustee's position under the trust relationship. If Li recognized this transfer, the trustee under the trust relationship would change from the investment company to Shao as an individual.

(B) Whether the Investment Company Had Contractual or Legal Basis to Transfer the "Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement" to Shao

According to Articles 5.2 to 5.3 of the "Trust Contract" involved, only in cases where the trustee dies or is unable to perform trust business normally must the trustee designate a lawyer or other custodian to act on its behalf, subject to confirmation by the committee. The investment company did not prove that the stipulated circumstances occurred. Moreover, according to the contract, even if a designation were necessary, it could only be a lawyer or other institution, not another natural person. Article 30, Paragraph 1 of the "Trust Law" provides that if the trust document provides otherwise or if there are compelling reasons, the trustee may entrust another person to handle trust affairs; Article 400 of the "Contract Law" also provides that in an emergency to protect the principal's interests, the trustee may sub-entrust without the principal's consent, but the trustee shall be liable for the actions of the sub-entrusted third party. The investment company did not prove that there were compelling reasons or emergencies requiring the sub-entrustment of trust matters to Shao in order to protect Li's interests. Therefore, the investment company's sub-entrustment of trust affairs to Shao as an individual without Li's consent, thereby extricating itself from the position of trustee under the trust relationship and transferring the trustee's position to Shao, had no basis either under the terms of the "Trust Contract" or under relevant legal provisions.

(C) Whether the Investment Company's Signing of the Transfer Agreement Constituted Malicious Collusion

Whether there is malicious collusion between parties can often be determined by examining external circumstances and the parties' external conduct. In this regard, the court makes the following comprehensive analysis:

First, before or at the time of signing the transfer agreement, was there a clear communication of intent between Shao and Luo to harm Li's interests? Li and the technology company argued that Luo admitted that he knew about Shao's removal from the technology company one week before signing the transfer agreement, and that his signing of the transfer agreement with Shao on behalf of the investment company under these circumstances constituted malicious collusion. The court holds: Since the technology company is one of the committee representatives, and Shao, who had long served as a senior executive of the technology company and the committee, was removed from his position as a senior executive of the technology company, this would inevitably have some impact on the operation of the committee and even the trust plan. If Luo knew of this in advance or at the time and still signed the transfer agreement with Shao, it would, to some extent, affect the determination of malicious collusion. The court notes that the investment company's defense statement signed by Luo stated that Shao approached Luo in early November 2020, mentioning that he had been removed from the position of chairman of the technology company. A week later, Shao again approached Luo, asking him to cooperate in signing the relevant transfer agreement. However, according to the "Statement of Facts" also signed by Luo, it stated that Shao approached Luo on November 13, 2020, asking him to cooperate in signing the relevant transfer agreement. Only later did a company employee contact Luo, stating that Shao had already been removed from the chairmanship of the technology company in July 2020. Therefore, regarding whether Luo knew about Shao's removal before or at the time of signing the transfer agreement, the defense statement and the "Statement of Facts," both signed by Luo, provide inconsistent accounts, which cannot constitute an admission of malicious collusion between the investment company and Shao.

Second, whether the provision for a gratuitous transfer harmed the interests of Li and the technology company, thereby becoming an important basis for determining malicious collusion. Li argued that the investment company's gratuitous transfer of the "Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement" to Shao clearly violated commercial rules and transaction practices, was extremely unreasonable, and could lead to an inference of malicious collusion between them. The court notes that the investment company transferred the rights and obligations under the "Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement" as a whole, rather than unilaterally transferring the investment company's physical property at zero consideration. That is, after Shao accepted the "Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement," he still bore the obligation to cash out trust interests. Li and the technology company also acknowledged that the investment company transferred the rights and obligations under the agreement, not actual physical property. During the proceedings, Shao also explicitly promised that he would continue to cash out relevant trust interests and would handle withdrawal matters for trustees applying for exit in accordance with the contract. Therefore, while the investment company's unauthorized transfer of the "Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement" was improper, considering that the "Trust Contract" was not terminated by the signing of the transfer agreement, and the investment company's obligations under the "Trust Contract" still existed, and the transferee Shao also explicitly promised to continue cashing out relevant trust interests. Based on existing evidence, it has not been shown that Shao's acceptance of the rights and obligations under the "Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement" has resulted in existing contracted employees being unable to realize trust interests or new employees being unable to sign new "Trust Contracts" due to Shao's actions. In summary, the investment company's zero-consideration transfer of the agreement to Shao cannot prove that the interests of Li and the technology company have been harmed, and cannot be used to prove malicious collusion between the parties. Moreover, the investment company transferred the agreement gratuitously, and Shao still promised to assume the cashing-out obligations. Without further evidence, it cannot be proven that the investment company and Shao obtained improper benefits.

Article 86, paragraph 1, of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Proceedings provides that if the parties' proof of facts concerning fraud, duress, malicious collusion, and proof of facts concerning oral wills or gifts lead the people's court to be convinced that the possibility of the existence of the facts to be proved can exclude reasonable doubt, the facts shall be deemed to exist. Considering comprehensively the aforementioned factors, namely, that Shao had actually accepted the entrustment of Mou Investment Company for a relatively long period of time to manage the trust property, had previously collected relevant trust subscription monies on its behalf, there is no evidence to prove that before or at the time of signing the transfer agreement, the parties had explicit or implicit communication of intent to harm Li's interests, and there is no evidence to prove that the transfer had caused or was sufficient to cause actual loss to Li and Mou Technology Company, or that Mou Investment Company and Shao had thereby obtained improper benefits. This Court is of the opinion that the act of Mou Investment Company signing the transfer agreement with Shao constitutes an unauthorized transfer of the trustee status under the trust relationship to Shao, but the proof that Mou Investment Company and Shao had malicious collusion has not yet reached the level of excluding reasonable doubt.

5. Determination of Validity of the Transfer Agreement (USD 50 Million)

Article 2 of the Trust Law of the PRC provides that a trust refers to an act in which the settlor, based on trust in the trustee, entrusts his property rights to the trustee, and the trustee manages or disposes of the property in his own name according to the settlor's wishes for the benefit of the beneficiary or for specific purposes. This provision demonstrates that the settlor's trust in the trustee is the cornerstone of the trust relationship, and the trustee's personal handling of trust affairs is the basis for maintaining such trust. Article 30, paragraph 1, of the Trust Law of the PRC, which provides that the trustee shall handle trust affairs personally unless otherwise stipulated in the trust documents or there are compelling reasons, clearly reflects this principle. Article 400 of the Contract Law of the PRC, effective at the time of the parties' conduct, provides that the agent shall personally handle the entrusted affairs, and with the consent of the principal, the agent may sub-entrust. If the sub-entrustment is not consented to, the agent shall bear liability for the acts of the third party in the sub-entrustment. The above provisions all reflect the value orientation of maintaining the basis of the principal's trust in the agent and protecting the principal's interests to the greatest extent. In fact, Article 1.7 of the Trust Contract involved in the case also expressly stipulates that the trustee is a person who manages the stock rights of the trustor in his own name based on the trust of the trustor, and the contract specifically refers to Mou Investment Company and Company A. The above provisions and contractual stipulations all demonstrate the importance of trust in the trust relationship.

Mou Investment Company, without the consent of the settlor, unauthorizedly transferred its trustee status under the trust relationship. After Li's trustee under the trust relationship was actually changed to Shao individually, Li's basis of trust in the trust involved in the case would undoubtedly be affected. Whether pursuant to Article 169, paragraph 1, of the General Provisions of the Civil Law of the PRC, which provides that if an agent needs to sub-entrust a third party for agency, the consent or ratification of the principal shall be obtained, and paragraph 3, which provides that if the sub-entrustment is not consented to or ratified by the principal, the agent shall bear liability for the acts of the third party in the sub-entrustment, or pursuant to Article 171, paragraph 1, of the same law, which provides that if an actor performs an agency act exceeding the scope of agency authority, it shall not be effective against the principal unless ratified by the principal, in this case, from the perspective of maximizing protection of Li's interests as the settlor and maintaining the stability of the trust structure, it is not appropriate to declare the act of signing the transfer agreement involved in the case as invalid outright; instead, Li and Mou Technology Company should be granted a choice. Shao, entrusted by Mou Investment Company, actually engaged in financial management services and related work regarding the trust property for a long period. Li, based on consideration of his own interests, and Mou Technology Company, based on consideration of the stability of the trust structure and whether it is conducive to the development of Mou Technology Company, may choose to accept or not accept the act of Mou Investment Company transferring trustee status to Shao, and may choose to recognize or not recognize Shao's trustee status. Now, Li and Mou Technology Company have chosen to request this Court to declare the transfer agreement invalid, clearly indicating that they do not accept Mou Investment Company's expression of intent to change the trustee to Shao, and indicating that they do not trust or accept the new trustee. The transfer agreement involved in the case was not ratified by the settlor Li and shall be deemed invalid.

Article 56 of the Contract Law of the PRC provides that an invalid contract or a rescinded contract has no legal binding force from the outset. If a part of a contract is invalid without affecting the validity of other parts, the other parts shall remain valid. In this case, on the one hand, Mou Investment Company entrusted for investment and financial management the trust property and rights which included multiple employees. Each employee, when obtaining trust rights or withdrawing from the trust plan in accordance with the contract, can have his corresponding rights distinguished from those of other employees. On the other hand, Mou Investment Company transferred the entire "Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement" to Shao. Regarding the issue of partial invalidity or overall invalidity of the transfer agreement, considering that Mou Technology Company is the initiator of the entire trust plan and the setter of the trust creation conditions, the purpose of the trust plan is to provide long-term continuous incentives to current and future employees of Mou Technology Company, and the interests of the employee trustors are tied to the stability and development of Mou Technology Company, therefore, the adverse impact of Mou Investment Company's unauthorized transfer of its trustee status on individual employee trustors, the adverse impact on the overall trust plan of Mou Technology Company, and the relationship between these two types of adverse impacts are difficult to strictly distinguish. Considering the above factors, this Court holds that the adverse impacts caused by Mou Investment Company's unauthorized transfer of the "Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement" are indivisible, and the transfer agreement involved in the case shall be declared invalid as a whole.

In summary, although the factual grounds and legal basis of Li and Mou Technology Company regarding the existence of malicious collusion between the two defendants have not been supported by this Court, when making a negative evaluation of the validity of a contract, the legal provisions relied upon by the people's court are not necessarily limited to the legal provisions asserted by the parties. If the validity of a contract should be negatively evaluated under other legal provisions, the people's court may apply other legal provisions to negate the validity of the contract. Otherwise, it would increase the litigation burden on the parties and cause unnecessary waste of judicial resources. In accordance with Article 3 and Article 8 of the Law of the PRC on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations, Article 169, paragraphs 1 and 3, and Article 171, paragraph 1 of the General Provisions of the Civil Law of the PRC, Article 400 of the Contract Law of the PRC, Article 158 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, and Article 86, paragraph 1 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Proceedings, this Court renders the following judgment:

1. The "Agreement on the Transfer of the Entrusted Investment and Financial Management Agreement" signed between Shao and Mou Investment Co., Ltd. (P*Ltd.), involving a financial management amount of USD 50 million, is invalid;

2. All other claims of Li and Mou Technology Group Co., Ltd. are dismissed.

The case acceptance fee of RMB 1,641,730 shall be borne by Shao and Mou Investment Co., Ltd. (P*Ltd.).

This judgment is final.
